h1: Jackson-Pollock Body Fat Calculator (3-Site Skinfold Method)
description: Calculate body fat percentage with the Jackson-Pollock 3-site skinfold method. Enter your caliper readings to get body density, fat mass, lean mass, and ACE classification instantly.
answerSnippet: The Jackson-Pollock 3-site skinfold method estimates body fat % by summing skinfold measurements at chest + abdomen + thigh (men) or triceps + suprailiac + thigh (women), calculating body density with the JP regression equation, then applying the Siri formula: Body Fat % = ((4.95 / Db) − 4.50) × 100. For a 35-year-old male at 175 lb with skinfolds of 15 / 20 / 18 mm, result = 17.2% (ACE 'Fitness' range). Standard error: ±3.5% vs. hydrostatic weighing.
intro: The **Jackson-Pollock 3-site skinfold** method is the most validated low-cost field test for body fat estimation in exercise science. Developed by **Andrew Jackson and Michael Pollock** at the University of Houston (1978 for men; 1980 for women with Ward), it is the standard endorsed by the **NSCA** and **ACE** certification programs and is widely used by personal trainers and sports scientists. Enter your caliper readings in mm and this calculator outputs body density (via the Siri equation), body fat %, ACE classification, fat mass, and lean mass — all in US units (pounds).
keyTakeaway: A 35-year-old male at **175 lb** with skinfolds of 15 / 20 / 18 mm computes to **17.2% body fat** — the 'Fitness' category per ACE (men's Fitness range: 14–17%). The Jackson-Pollock method carries a standard error of ±3.5% versus hydrostatic weighing, making it one of the most accurate skinfold-based field protocols available.
useCases: Tracking body composition changes during a cut or bulk
Baseline fitness assessment before starting a new training program
Comparing body fat levels against ACE health classification standards
Estimating lean body mass to calculate daily protein targets
Monitoring fat loss progress more accurately than scale weight alone
Pre-competition body composition check for natural athletes
explanation:
## How the Jackson-Pollock 3-Site Method Works

The Jackson-Pollock method estimates body fat % by measuring the thickness of subcutaneous fat at three standardized anatomical sites with a skinfold caliper. The sum of those three measurements, combined with age, is fed into a sex-specific regression equation to compute body density (Db). Body density is then converted to a body fat percentage using the Siri two-compartment equation.

## The Formulas

```
// Step 1 — sum the three skinfolds
S = skinfold1 + skinfold2 + skinfold3  (mm)

// Step 2 — calculate body density
// Men (chest + abdominal + thigh) — Jackson & Pollock, 1978
Db = 1.10938 − (0.0008267 × S) + (0.0000016 × S²) − (0.0002574 × Age)

// Women (triceps + suprailiac + thigh) — Jackson, Pollock & Ward, 1980
Db = 1.0994921 − (0.0009929 × S) + (0.0000023 × S²) − (0.0001392 × Age)

// Step 3 — Siri equation (body fat %)
Body Fat % = ((4.95 / Db) − 4.50) × 100

// Step 4 — mass partitioning
Fat Mass  = Total Weight × (Body Fat % / 100)
Lean Mass = Total Weight − Fat Mass
```

## Worked Example — Male, 35 years, 175 lb

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Sex | Male |
| Age | 35 years |
| Chest skinfold | 15 mm |
| Abdominal skinfold | 20 mm |
| Thigh skinfold | 18 mm |
| **Sum (S)** | **53 mm** |
| Body density (Db) | **1.0647 g/mL** |
| **Body Fat %** | **17.2%** |
| Fat Mass | 30.1 lb |
| Lean Mass | 144.9 lb |
| ACE Classification | **Fitness** |

## ACE Body Fat Classification Reference Table

| Category | Men (%) | Women (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Essential fat | 2–5 | 10–13 |
| Athletes | 6–13 | 14–20 |
| Fitness | 14–17 | 21–24 |
| Average | 18–24 | 25–31 |
| Obese | ≥ 25 | ≥ 32 |

## Body Fat % by Sum of Skinfolds — Quick Reference (Men, Age 30)

This table shows how body fat % changes with skinfold sum for a typical 30-year-old male:

| Sum of 3 skinfolds (mm) | Body Density (g/mL) | Body Fat % | ACE Category |
|---|---|---|---|
| 30 mm | 1.0871 | 10.7% | Athlete |
| 45 mm | 1.0724 | 14.2% | Fitness |
| 60 mm | 1.0560 | 18.5% | Average |
| 75 mm | 1.0380 | 23.5% | Average |
| 90 mm | 1.0183 | 28.8% | Obese |
| 105 mm | 0.9969 | 34.7% | Obese |

## Measurement Technique

1. **Locate the site**: Use anatomical landmarks (for chest: diagonal fold midway between anterior axillary line and nipple; for abdomen: vertical fold 2 cm lateral to navel; for thigh: vertical fold midway between kneecap and inguinal fold).
2. **Pinch correctly**: Grasp a fold of skin and underlying subcutaneous fat only — not muscle — between thumb and index finger.
3. **Apply caliper**: Place caliper jaws 1 cm from your fingers, perpendicular to the fold.
4. **Read at 2 seconds**: Release the caliper lever and read the dial after 2 seconds (before the fold compresses further).
5. **Triple measure and average**: Take three readings per site and average them for reliability.

## Limitations to Know

- **Tester skill matters**: A ±1–2 mm error per site shifts results by 1–3 percentage points. Use the same trained tester for serial measurements.
- **Population validity**: Equations were validated on White adults aged 18–61. Accuracy may be reduced for other ethnic groups, older adults (> 65), or extreme athletes.
- **Hydration state**: Dehydration compresses skinfolds and can underestimate body fat by 2–4%.
- **Not a clinical substitute**: For medical decisions (surgery, bariatric screening), prefer DEXA or hydrostatic weighing.
- **Pregnancy / edema**: Do not apply to pregnant individuals or those with significant fluid retention.

faq.q: What sites do I measure for men vs. women?
faq.a: Men use chest, abdominal, and thigh. Women use triceps, suprailiac (just above the hip bone), and thigh. Measuring wrong sites produces invalid results — the regression equations are fitted to these exact anatomical locations.

faq.q: How accurate is the Jackson-Pollock 3-site method?
faq.a: With a trained tester, the standard error of estimate (SEE) is approximately ±3.5% body fat compared to hydrostatic weighing (the classic US gold standard). DEXA has an SEE of ±1.5–2%. JP3 is the most accurate commonly used skinfold protocol and is practical for repeated tracking.

faq.q: How do I measure a skinfold correctly?
faq.a: Pinch a fold of skin plus subcutaneous fat (not muscle) between thumb and index finger at the correct anatomical site, apply caliper jaws 1 cm from your fingers, release the lever, and read after 2 seconds. Take three readings and average them. Measurements should be taken on the right side of the body.

faq.q: What is the Siri equation and why is it used?
faq.a: Siri (1956) derived Body Fat % = ((4.95 / Db) − 4.50) × 100 from a two-compartment model, assuming fat density ≈ 0.9 g/mL and fat-free mass density ≈ 1.1 g/mL. It converts body density (which the JP regression predicts) into an interpretable body fat percentage. It remains the standard conversion in exercise science.

faq.q: What is a good body fat percentage for men?
faq.a: Per ACE standards: 2–5% is essential fat (minimum for survival); 6–13% is athlete-level; 14–17% is fitness; 18–24% is average; ≥ 25% is obese. For general health, 10–20% is considered healthy for adult men. Athletes competing in physique or endurance sports often target 6–12%.

faq.q: What is a healthy body fat percentage for women?
faq.a: Per ACE standards: 10–13% is essential fat; 14–20% is athlete-level; 21–24% is fitness; 25–31% is average; ≥ 32% is obese. Women naturally carry more fat than men due to hormonal and reproductive biology. For general health, 18–28% is considered a healthy range for adult women.

faq.q: Can I use this calculator if I'm over 60?
faq.a: The original equations were validated on adults aged 18–61. Older adults tend to accumulate more intra-muscular and visceral fat not captured by surface skinfolds, so the JP method tends to underestimate true body fat in this group. The results are still useful for trend tracking, but interpret the absolute percentages with caution.

faq.q: What does lean mass include — is it the same as muscle?
faq.a: No. Lean body mass (LBM) includes everything except fat: muscle, bone, organs, blood, connective tissue, and water. Skeletal muscle typically makes up 40–50% of lean mass in a healthy adult, so lean mass is significantly higher than muscle mass alone.

faq.q: Why does my result differ from a bioimpedance (BIA) scale?
faq.a: Bioimpedance is highly sensitive to hydration, meal timing, bladder fullness, and skin temperature. JP skinfolds and BIA use fundamentally different physical models. Discrepancies of 2–5% are common and expected — this does not mean one tool is 'wrong.' Use the same method consistently for progress tracking.

faq.q: Is lower body fat always better?
faq.a: No. Going below essential fat thresholds (< 5% men, < 10% women) is dangerous and can impair hormone production, immune function, and bone density. In women, extreme leanness can cause the Female Athlete Triad (low energy availability, menstrual disruption, bone loss). An optimal body fat range for health differs from competition-level leanness.

faq.q: How does this compare to the 7-site Jackson-Pollock method?
faq.a: The 7-site JP method measures chest, midaxillary, triceps, subscapular, abdomen, suprailiac, and thigh — providing higher accuracy (SEE ≈ ±3.0% vs ±3.5% for 3-site). The 3-site version trades a small amount of precision for speed and practicality, making it the preferred choice for routine fitness assessments.

example.title: Example: 30-year-old male, 175 lb, 3-site skinfolds
steps: **Sum of skinfolds**: 15 + 20 + 18 = 53 mm across the three sites.
**Body density**: the Jackson-Pollock 3-site equation gives about 1.06234 g/mL.
**Body fat %**: applying the Siri equation yields 16% body fat (Fitness range).
**Mass split**: 16% of 175 lb ≈ 27.9 lb fat, leaving 147.1 lb lean mass.
